title: How does sealing interact with generics and wildcards?
shortTitle: How does sealing interact with generics and wildcards?
keyPoints: A sealed type can declare type parameters, and the permits clause names classes, not parameterized types.
Sealing closes the set of subtype classes while generics parameterize the data each carries; they constrain different things.
Because generics are erased at runtime, the PermittedSubclasses attribute records raw class names, and the closed set is class-level.
An exhaustive switch over a wildcard-typed sealed generic still only needs to cover the permitted classes, not the type arguments.
Pattern-match generic sealed types with wildcard patterns like `BuyOrder<?>` because the type argument is erased at runtime.
Sealing plus generics is a clean way to model type-safe heterogeneous results like Result<T> with Success<T> and Failure<T>.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sealing closes the set of subtype classes while generics parameterize the data each carries, so the closed set and exhaustive matching hold regardless of type arguments or wildcards.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Sealed generic type** – a sealed interface or class with a type parameter, e.g., `sealed interface Order<T> permits BuyOrder, SellOrder`.
- **Permits names classes** – the `permits` clause lists class names, not parameterized types, because generics are erased.
- **Exhaustiveness by class** – a `switch` is exhaustive when every permitted class is covered, regardless of type arguments.
- **Wildcard patterns** – match with `BuyOrder<?>` because the exact type argument is not recoverable at runtime.
- **Type-safe modeling** – `Result<T>` with `Success<T>` and `Failure<T>` gives exhaustive handling with typed payloads.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India having a sealed set of order tickets: BuyOrder and SellOrder. Each ticket is stamped with the instrument it trades: equity, bond, or currency. The sealed rule fixes that there are exactly two ticket shapes. The generic parameter is the instrument stamp. A wildcard means "any ticket regardless of instrument." The closed set of two shapes stays closed no matter which instrument stamp is on them.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Sealed Generic Hierarchy:

  sealed Order<T extends Instrument>
       │
       ├── BuyOrder<T>       (keeps T generic)
       ├── SellOrder<T>      (keeps T generic)
       └── EquityMarketOrder (fixes T = Equity)

  Exhaustiveness:

  switch (order) {
    case BuyOrder<?>          → handled
    case SellOrder<?>         → handled
    case EquityMarketOrder    → handled
    // No default: all 3 classes covered
  }

  Type arguments erased at runtime:
  BuyOrder<Equity> → BuyOrder (raw class)
  BuyOrder<Bond>   → BuyOrder (same raw class)
  Exhaustiveness checks classes, not type args
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sealing and generics constrain different things and work together cleanly. Sealing closes the set of subtype classes. Generics parameterize the data each subtype carries. The `permits` clause names classes, not parameterized types, because generics are erased. The `PermittedSubclasses` attribute stores raw class names, so the closed set is at the class level.

The key interaction for pattern matching is that an exhaustive `switch` over a wildcard-typed sealed generic only needs to cover the permitted classes, not the possible type arguments. You match with `BuyOrder<?>` because the type argument is erased at runtime. This gives compiler-checked handling of every order action while keeping the instrument data type-safe at the API boundary.

At National Bank of India, Rajesh modeled trading orders as a generic sealed interface `Order<T extends Instrument>` with `BuyOrder` and `SellOrder`. The risk engine accepted `Order<? extends Instrument>` to process any order, and the exhaustive switch covered both classes with no default. For the `Result<T>` pattern, `Success<T>` and `Failure<T>` gave exhaustive handling with typed payloads.

Remember one sentence: sealing closes the family of classes, generics type the payload, and the exhaustive switch holds regardless of type arguments because the closed set is at the class level.
